pr_title: scripts: build: gen_isr_tables: make bit masks configurable
pr_body:
Some architectures such as RISC-V support more than 255 interrupts per aggrigator. This diff adds the ability to forgo the aggrigator pattern and use a configurable number of bits for multilevel interruts.

Fixes #11274 (partially)
Fixes #61136
pr_comments:
Looks good - it might be better to call the option `1ST_LEVEL_INTERRUPT_BITS` to be a "bit" more descriptive 😏

Would be good to get a testcase as well. Do you think the `adp_xc7k_ae350` would make a good candidate board?

> `adp_xc7k_ae350`

I read your comment wrong at first. I can make the name change! As for the board, do you have one laying around? I had been thinking to buy an andes board, but I haven't yet.

> > `adp_xc7k_ae350`
> 
> I read your comment wrong at first. I can make the name change! As for the board, do you have one laying around? I had been thinking to buy an andes board, but I haven't yet.

@jgl-meta  I just assumed they were unobtainium. It should be a build-only test though, so no need for physical HW.

> This is not going to work. For example, all multiple level interrupts support assume 8 bits per level. So runtime functions like `irq_from_level_2()` and `irq_get_level()` are going to give incorrect values.

Ah yeah. Thanks for catching that. I will fix it.

You will probably need to modify the device tree side also to generate the correct IRQ numbers as they are also assuming 8 bits per level. And also documentation (https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/kernel/services/interrupts.html#multi-level-interrupt-handling) needs to be updated.

Though, IIRC, the device tree side has an assumption that a single 32-bit integer can encode all 3 levels of interrupts. So your change will conflict with that assumption.

> You will probably need to modify the device tree side also to generate the correct IRQ numbers as they are also assuming 8 bits per level. And also documentation (https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/kernel/services/interrupts.html#multi-level-interrupt-handling) needs to be updated.
> 
> Though, IIRC, the device tree side has an assumption that a single 32-bit integer can encode all 3 levels of interrupts. So your change will conflict with that assumption.

I don't think that is exactly true. You can see the script will error out in the event the bits used are actually greater than 32. In fact, there is nothing currently enforcing the MAX_IRQ_PER_AGGREGATOR to respect fitting nicely inside it's space allotted. Meaning it is up to the end user to know and respect those boundaries. Furthermore,  I believe it is the case that the script is currently somewhat broken, aside from not respect boundaries, for example RISC-V can have 1024 interrupts for a single aggregator per the spec with a maximum of two levels of interrupts, but this is not possible to handle in the current script. Ideally, what I believe would be optimal to addressing these problems is giving the option for CPUs to more precisely define their interrupt levels, without changing the current schema, which is what I am attempting here.

Additionally, I think it is worth noting here, I don't see any boards in the main repo that are utilizing a really large number of interrupts, so it may be the case that we are some of the first to struggle with this problem.

Still, how multi-level interrupt is encoded is in the document. So if you need to deviate from that, you will need to document it thoroughly, and provide defaults that work the same as before.

TBH, a hierarchy of interrupt nodes would be better than encoding all levels in an integer. One just needs to traverse node "upwards" to enable all necessary interrupts. That would get rid of the per-level limitation, and also allow more levels. That would be a rather huge change for everyone so some brave soul will need to tackle it.
Hm... come to think of it... should those defaults in kconfigs be 8 bits to mimic the current behavior?

> Still, how multi-level interrupt is encoded is in the document. So if you need to deviate from that, you will need to document it thoroughly, and provide defaults that work the same as before.
> 
> TBH, a hierarchy of interrupt nodes would be better than encoding all levels in an integer. One just needs to traverse node "upwards" to enable all necessary interrupts. That would get rid of the per-level limitation, and also allow more levels. That would be a rather huge change for everyone so some brave soul will need to tackle it.

Definitely agree that it should be documented, I will do so once this gets closer. This change is more of an addition than changing the way it entirely works though. The intent of writing it the way I think it is now was to not have an effect unless the fields are set. Not setting them should default to the script working exactly how it is now. 

As for the hierarchy approach you speak of. I also agree that it would be better. However, as you point out that is a very large change. I am not opposed to working toward something like that if there is support for it. I am also interested in hearing your ideas on how to reconcile that approach with the current implementation. Or your ideas for getting started on such a venture.

> Hm... come to think of it... should those defaults in kconfigs be 8 bits to mimic the current behavior?
 
I am honestly not sure. I think the fact that it is configurable seems to point to the fact it shouldn't matter.

> As for the hierarchy approach you speak of. I also agree that it would be better. However, as you point out that is a very large change. I am not opposed to working toward something like that if there is support for it. I am also interested in hearing your ideas on how to reconcile that approach with the current implementation. Or your ideas for getting started on such a venture.

I would think half of the changes would be related to code and data generation from devicetree. In very simple terms, you will need to create a tree where each node contains a device node pointer to the controller, a IRQ number, pointer to parent controller and ref count. When en-/dis-abling interrupts, it does the usual on the controller, and if there is a parent, tell parent to enable that interrupt (and so on). For non-leaf nodes, the ref count is there to avoid disabling a parent interrupt if children are still using them. You can then get rid of the "IRQ next level" API. The other half of the changes would be to update the drivers to utilize the new scheme.

> TBH, a hierarchy of interrupt nodes would be better than encoding all levels in an integer.

Yeah.  This code is getting increasingly crufty, and it's never been integrated well with DTS.  I'm actually struggling with it right now for a mt8195 audio DSP integration (which is a really simple interrupt controller scheme!) and it's... sorta unpleasant.

In an ideal world, we'd just take the DAG of controller nodes out of devicetree (almost all the info is already there) and automatically generate all the handling that currently has to be done manually in kconfig (usually duplicating info already in dts).

> @andyross - do you have any wish-list items?

Having literally just suffered through this again, boy do I:

1. Eliminate all the `*_2ND_LEVEL_*` kconfig nonsense.  (Actually eliminate all the kconfig dependence here, as much as I hate DTS syntax this is 100% a DTS problem, it's not software configuration).

2. Enumerate the graph of interrupt_parent pointers in DTS to ensure it's a dag that points to a single top-level interrupt controller.

3. No more bitmasks, tight-pack the graph into a depth-first array or whatever, such that each interrupt has a unique spot and the "IRQN" number is identical with the _sw_isr_table[] offset.

4. Some DT macro hackery to give each controller its offset within that table as a compile time constant, and in the reverse direction generate a function or table to give each controller an O(fast) predicate to choose a child controller given an input interrupt.

5. Auto generate the glue logic that right now lives (usually) in the SOC code: Zephyr's irq_enable/disable/is_enabled() functions should be handled by this layer, and call directly into the associated controller drivers.  Platform authors shouldn't have to write code to duplicate what DTS already knows.
I guess one last thing I might throw out there is whether or not we deprecate `CONFIG_MAX_IRQ_PER_AGGREGATOR`

> This looks fine to me, with the caveat noted above that what I really want to see is a ground-up rewrite. :) But this is a very reasonable extension of the current scheme that shouldn't break anything or confuse anyone (more than we already are, anyway).

@andyross Should I try to put together an RFC?
@tejlmand could you take a look?

> Some offline reviews saying `irq_get_level()` was a bit difficult to read, so I would suggest the `IS_ENABLED()` approach. The compiler is still able to optimize. https://godbolt.org/z/WMW81xrch

I think I had initially opted against this because I was thinking to make the Kconfig options opt-outable. Since they aren't I think this should work now let me see if I can get the changes going.

issue_context.title: gen_isr_tables: unable to support riscv plic interrupt mapping
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
Currently, in a multi-level (nested) interrupt controller arrangement, the maximum number of IRQs supported for a given level is silently hard-coded with a few "magic numbers".

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/scripts/build/gen_isr_tables.py#L18-L28

The per-level limit set in Python is 255. However, some architectures (RISC-V being one of them) have a standard interrupt controller design that supports far more than 255.

Directly from the RISC-V PLIC specification, this standard interrupt controller supports 1023 IRQs locally (so significantly more than 255).

https://github.com/riscv/riscv-plic-spec/blob/master/riscv-plic.adoc#memory-map

Moreover, there are many boards in Zephyr which already include a PLIC in their Devicetree.

```shell
# likely some duplication, but there are many plics..
grep "plic" $(find boards soc arch -name '*.dts' -o -name '*.dtsi') | wc -l
157
```

Namely, `adp_xc7k_ae350` ([andes_v5_ae350.dtsi](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/dts/riscv/andes/andes_v5_ae350.dtsi#L179))

This is a bit of "a big deal" because Zephyr is unable to accomadate a fundamental feature of most RISC-V designs. Luckily it is 95% a configuration and build issue.

Please also mention any information which could help others to understand
the problem you're facing:
 - What target platform are you using? `adp_xc7k_ae350`
 - What have you tried to diagnose or workaround this issue? added to the testsuite and found the root cause of the error
 - Is this a regression? Likely not.

**To Reproduce**
Add the test case ~~in the linked PR~~ Linked at the bottom of this issue. Optionally, make the modifications mentioned below to increase verbosity of `gen_isr_tables.py`.
1. `west build -p auto -b adp_xc7k_ae350 -T tests/kernel/gen_isr_table/arch.interrupt.gen_isr_table.riscv64.multi_level`
2. See error

**Expected behavior**
1. The build to succeed without issue.
2. The interrupt is routed and available to SW at the given IRQ

**Impact**
It's actually a bit of a showstopper.

**Logs and console output**
